new.title: Constraining Intergalactic Dust with Supernova Color Evolution: Current Constraints from DES and Forecasts for LSST and Roman
new.summary: Dust is an important systematic in precision Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) cosmology, and while dust in the Milky Way and SN host galaxies has been extensively studied, the impact of potential intergalactic dust is less well constrained. Using estimates from B. Ménard et al. (2010), we find that current intergalactic dust bounds could shift SN distance moduli by up to 0.02 mag at $z \gtrsim 1$ from simulations. However, we show dust models can be constrained independently by SN samples themselves via a specific predicted redshift-dependent evolution observed in SN colors. While current data from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) cannot distinguish between various amounts of intergalactic dust in our universe, we demonstrate that the Roman Space Telescope (Roman) will place a significant constraint on intergalactic dust models ($>$ 3$\sigma$). In contrast, the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), even with its unprecedented statistics, will only reach $\lesssim$ 2$\sigma$ significance on any given intergalactic dust prediction relative to no dust. We propagate multiple parameterizations of intergalactic dust through to cosmology. For LSST, we see a $\sim$60% reduction in the figure of merit (FoM) for $w$CDM and a $\sim$20% reduction for $w_0w_a$CDM, and for Roman, a $\sim$20% reduction in the FoM for $w$CDM and a $\sim$5% reduction for $w_0w_a$CDM. Utilizing Roman as an external constraint on dust for LSST results in a slightly improved FoM ($\sim$50% reduction) for $w$CDM for LSST. Finally, we show that intergalactic dust uncertainties decrease the FoM of the previous DES analysis (16.9% for $w$CDM and 8.1% for $w_0w_a$CDM) and that intergalactic dust cannot explain away recent hints for evolving dark energy.

new.title: CHEX-MATE: Probing the thermal$-$non-thermal connection in radio halo clusters with LoTSS-DR2
new.summary: The main baryonic component of galaxy clusters is in the form of a hot plasma observed in the X-rays. In addition, clusters host a non-thermal component (relativistic particles and magnetic fields) which is studied mainly via radio telescopes and is dynamically coupled to the thermal plasma. These two components evolve together within the system and are subject to both micro and macro-physical processes which can be traced only with deep and detailed observations. We present the first homogeneous spatially resolved radio--X-ray study of 18 radio halo clusters combining CHEX-MATE and the LOFAR Two metre Sky Survey DR2. Radio ($I_R$) and X-ray ($I_X$) surface brightness are clearly correlated (Spearman coefficient $r_s \ge 0.5$), following a typically sublinear $I_R-I_X$ relation ($67 \pm 5\%$ of the sample) that appears to be independent of other cluster properties, although a tentative trend with mass/redshift may be worth exploring with larger samples. When inspecting such a relation as a function of the radius, we observe a variety of behaviours, which suggest that the interplay between the thermal and non-thermal plasma components varies with radius. We find the averaged slope profile of dynamically disturbed clusters to be consistent with expectations from turbulent re-acceleration models where a constant ratio between cosmic-ray electron and thermal energy densities is assumed. Differently, less perturbed clusters require an increasing cosmic-ray-to-thermal energy ratio with radius. Finally, we show that radio halo surface-brightness profiles can be effectively rescaled using X-ray information and theoretical expectations. This procedure significantly reduces their scatter and reveals common underlying trends based on the cluster dynamics, resembling what is observed for the thermal ICM, and strengthening the idea of a strong interplay between these two plasma components.

new.title: Acoustic Priors from the Latest Cosmic Microwave Background Data
new.summary: We revisit the physics of the acoustic peaks and illustrate how early-Universe information in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) can be disentangled from late-time signatures imprinted by gravitational lensing and the integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect. Applying this separation to Planck PR4, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 temperature and polarization data combined with the joint lensing reconstruction, we update the model-independent constraints on the angular acoustic scale and the physical densities, $100\theta_*=1.04100\pm0.00021$, $\omega_{\rm b}=(2.2440\pm0.0099)\times10^{-2}$, and $\omega_{\rm bc}=0.1410\pm0.0011$. These constraints are consistent with the previous Planck PR4-only analysis and remain stable for extended late-time cosmologies beyond $\Lambda$CDM. Adding ACT DR6 to the combination favors a higher $\omega_{\rm b}$ and, through their correlation, a higher primordial tilt $n_{\rm s}$ than PR4 alone. The reconstructed lensing spectrum exceeds that of $\Lambda$CDM, with two features near $L\simeq50$ and $L\sim10^3$, and the excess is reduced when WMAP replaces the Planck primary spectra. Marginalizing over the lensing-induced peak smoothing, rather than tying it to the late-time model, lowers the preference of the CMB and DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) for $w_0w_a$CDM over $\Lambda$CDM from $3.0\sigma$ to $1.9\sigma$, or from $3.2\sigma$ to $2.4\sigma$ when Union3.1 supernovae are added. We further use the acoustic prior to predict BAO distances from CMB data alone under several late-time expansion histories, testing their consistency with DESI measurements assuming standard pre-recombination physics.

new.title: No Cluster Left Behind I: Joint Mass Calibration for Dark Energy Survey and South Pole Telescope Clusters
new.summary: Multiwavelength observations of galaxy clusters are among the most promising probes of the growth of structure and dark energy. Optically identified clusters have a high number density and can thus probe the halo mass function well into the group regime, but their weak-lensing mass calibration suffers from a selection bias induced by line-of-sight projection effects. Clusters detected via their intracluster medium (ICM) -- through X-ray emission or the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect (SZe) -- are less affected by such selection biases, but current survey sensitivity restricts ICM-selected samples to high-mass systems. Previous multiwavelength analyses tend to limit to clusters with millimeter detections and thus to the high-mass population. In this paper, we propose a flexible modeling framework in which all clusters from multiwavelength surveys can be combined and modeled, even if they are detected in only one survey. As a pilot study, we jointly model richness and lensing of clusters from the Dark Energy Survey and the SZe signal from the South Pole Telescope. This approach yields precise cluster mass calibration while self-consistently constraining optical selection biases. We have found a $\sim$20% bias in the large-scale lensing signal of clusters selected by richness, and a bias ranging from $\sim-20$% at low richness to zero at high richness for clusters selected by both richness and SZe. Compared to current approaches, this framework is highly scalable and readily extensible, paving the way for the full utilization of multiwavelength cluster data in next-generation surveys.

new.title: Inference of Cosmic Dawn and Reionization Parameters from the 21 cm Global Spectrum Measurement of the DSL Mission
new.summary: The 21 cm global spectrum is an important observable for cosmic dawn and epoch of reionization. The Discovering the Sky at the Longest Wavelengths mission (DSL, also known as Hongmeng), will measure the 21 cm global spectrum from the lunar orbit, thus avoiding the systematic effects common in ground based experiments, potentially producing the most accurate measurement to date. In this paper, we present a Bayesian inference framework, and investigate the constraints that can be placed on the cosmic dawn and reionization model parameters, either from the 21 cm global spectrum data alone, or from its combination with 21\,cm spatial power-spectrum data. For the global spectrum data, we assume a residual error equivalent to the thermal noise of a total observation of 30, 300, or 3000 orbit cycles of DSL. For the power spectrum, we adopt representative forecasts for HERA or SKA-Low. We find that there is generally a degeneracy between the foreground and the 21 cm global signal, and one has to make some restrictions on the form of either the foreground or the 21 cm global spectrum to break this degeneracy. Using the physically motivated emulator 21cmEMU, we generate the 21 cm global spectrum and power spectrum under a common astrophysical parameterization, while marginalizing over the foreground parameters. We derive constraints for two representative models, with their global spectrum absorption minimum at 105 and 94 MHz respectively. With only the global spectrum data, there remains much degeneracy in the astrophysical parameters. We find that the spatial power spectrum is highly complementary to the global spectrum, which can break the degeneracy and tighten up the constraints significantly.

new.title: Multiwavelength Analysis of the Merging Cluster RM J121917.6+505432.8: A Three-way Merger in Disguise?
new.summary: We identify the galaxy cluster RM J121917.6+505432.8 as a candidate bimodal merging cluster due to its optical properties listed in the redMaPPer cluster catalog. To confirm the cluster's merging state and reveal its dark matter halo and intracluster medium (ICM) morphologies, we conducted a multiwavelength follow-up campaign encompassing HST/ACS optical observations, XMM-Newton X-ray imaging, and Keck/Deimos multislit spectroscopy. The weak lensing mass reconstruction performed with the HST images shows two resolved peaks whose positions coincide with the two brightest cluster galaxies. The ICM morphology is consistent with a post-pericenter merger, with significant asymmetry in X-ray flux between subclusters. Our Keck/Deimos redshift measurements reveal a relative velocity $\Delta v_{\mathrm{LOS}} = 480$ km s$^{-1}$ between eastern and western subclusters. The eastern, more massive subcluster, however, exhibits a highly elongated shape, suggesting either a dark matter halo of considerable eccentricity or the presence of a third, unresolved halo, eliciting the question of whether RMJ1219 is truly binary or a three-way merger. To investigate these hypotheses, we fit the weak lensing shear data using four different combinations of spherical and elliptical NFW halo models and provide an estimate of the mass and concentration of each subhalo. Although the best fit is achieved with a three-halo model, the data are insufficient to determine whether the introduction of extra parameters is statistically justified.

new.title: Halo spin-axis correlations in IllustrisTNG: Lagrangian-to-Eulerian separation mapping, baryonic effects, and redshift-space distortions
new.summary: We investigate correlations of halo and stellar spin axes in the TNG300 volume of the IllustrisTNG simulations and compare them with a model based on linear tidal torque theory (LTTT). Dark matter (DM) halo spin axes at $z = 0$ exhibit positive correlations as a function of Lagrangian pair separation. The LTTT-based model describes their separation dependence well, with weak variation in the fitted amplitude across mass thresholds. A Lagrangian-to-Eulerian separation mapping based on the conditional distributions of initial separations at fixed present-day separation, measured directly from the simulations, allows the model to reproduce the overall trends in both real and redshift space without additional fitting. The hydrodynamic and DM-only runs generally show similar DM halo spin-axis correlations, although the DM-only run exhibits a steeper rise at small real-space separations. In the hydrodynamic run, stellar spin-axis correlations are consistent with the same Lagrangian form as their DM halo counterparts, but with approximately 60% of the DM correlation amplitudes. Positive stellar correlations persist in both real and redshift space, and the mapped model captures their separation dependence. Initial spin-axis correlations of protohalos are substantially stronger than their present-day counterparts at the same Lagrangian separations, consistent with subsequent nonlinear spin evolution weakening these correlations. These results suggest that present-day halo and stellar spin-axis correlations retain signatures of the initial tidal field and that their general behavior can be understood through LTTT-based modeling combined with pair-separation mapping.

new.title: Small-scale priors for large-scale cosmology: the case of $b_ϕ$
new.summary: Perturbative descriptions of galaxy clustering introduce free bias parameters that capture the complex physics of galaxy formation. Local primordial non-Gaussianity (PNG), parametrized by $f_{NL}$, induces a scale-dependent contribution to the galaxy bias that is proportional to $f_{NL} b_\phi$, where $b_\phi$ quantifies how galaxy formation responds to PNG. Accurately determining $b_{\phi}$ is therefore essential for robust constraints on $f_{NL}$. Current analyses usually adopt a modified universal relation, $b_\phi = 2\delta_c(b_1-p)$, with $p$ calibrated to simulations. This relies on the accuracy of the simulated galaxy-formation model and ignores the uncertainty on $b_\phi$, potentially biasing $f_{NL}$ constraints. We investigate whether $b_\phi$ can be constrained from small-scale galaxy clustering using a flexible empirical galaxy-formation model. We fit an extended Subhalo Abundance Matching (SHAMe) model to small-scale clustering measurements and combine it with dark-matter-only separate-universe simulations to infer a posterior on $b_\phi$. We validate the method using IllustrisTNG hydrodynamical separate-universe simulations. Without calibration on hydrodynamical simulations, SHAMe predicts $b_\phi$ with a median error of 10%, compared with 38% for a fixed halo occupation distribution (HOD) that neglects the occupation response to $\phi$, and 23% for the universality relation. The residual error is dominated by central galaxies near the selection threshold and persists when using the true stellar-mass assignment conditioned on the same subhalo properties. Small-scale clustering combined with a subhalo-based empirical model predicts most of galaxy-abundance response to local PNG. The remainder depends on galaxy-formation physics and should enter $b_\phi$ priors as a theoretical uncertainty. This provides a route to data-informed priors on bias parameters.

new.title: Scaling and Cross-Simulation Generalization of Graph Neural Networks for Cosmic-Web Classification in CAMELS
new.summary: Graph-based methods can classify galaxies by their dark-matter cosmic-web environments, but reliability beyond development simulations remains uncertain. Galaxy-formation models alter tracer populations and spatial distributions, potentially shifting graph features. We test how graph neural networks scale with independent training realizations and transfer across hydrodynamical simulations. Using the $z=0$ CAMELS IllustrisTNG, SIMBA and Astrid suites, we label galaxies with $M_\star>10^9\,M_\odot$ as void, sheet, filament or knot from the smoothed cold-dark-matter density field. We represent their spatial distributions as periodic Delaunay graphs with ten geometric descriptors. We compare a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and five graph neural networks (GNNs), including a local graph Transformer, under realization-grouped evaluation. Learning curves increase training data from 10 to 100 realizations, with validation and test boxes fixed. We test every source-to-target suite pairing on 100 unseen realizations per target suite. On this external holdout, the Transformer, GAT+ and EdgeConv reach mean per-realization macro-averaged F1 scores of $0.652$, $0.651$ and $0.642$, against $0.481$ for the MLP. The Transformer outperforms the MLP by 0.171, while the difference between the Transformer and GAT+ is not statistically significant. Voids remain the hardest class. Performance is higher in boxes with more selected galaxies and shorter Delaunay edges. Associations with cosmological and feedback parameters weaken after accounting for galaxy richness and void fraction. Our results benchmark the scaling and cross-simulation transfer of galaxy-graph classifiers, demonstrating the value of neighbourhood information and identifying tracer sampling as an important limitation for dark-matter web inference.

new.title: Physical quasar pairs in DESI DR1 as tracers of protoclusters at $z\approx2$
new.summary: Close pairs of quasars at the same redshift are expected to mark overdense regions that will collapse into galaxy clusters. Earlier work with SDSS found about 2800 such pairs, too few to follow their environment with separation. We build the largest sample of physical quasar pairs to date from DESI DR1 and test whether pairs out to Mpc separations trace protoclusters. We select pairs with rest-frame velocity difference $|\Delta V|\leq900 km/s$ and projected separation $r_p\leq4$~Mpc at $1.2\leq z\leq2.8$, measure their purity and fibre completeness, and measure the clustering of pair members around all DESI quasars. We find 40\,626 physical pairs with projected separation $r_p\leq2.5$~Mpc, where their purity falls to 50\%, the effective radius of protoclusters at $z\approx2$. Pair members are $1.69\pm0.14$, $1.78\pm0.09$ and $2.01\pm0.06$ times more clustered than all quasars for projected separations $r_p\leq1$, 1--2.5 and 2.5--4~Mpc, while chance pairs show little excess ($1.08\pm0.05$). This corresponds to haloes of $\sim1.4$--$2.2\times10^{13}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$. Physical quasar pairs with projected separations up to 2.5~Mpc trace protocluster environments, at the level that AbacusSummit mocks predict in $\Lambda$CDM. The full DESI survey will turn them into a statistical census of protoclusters at cosmic noon.

new.title: Galaxy cluster thermodynamic profiles beyond self-similarity
new.summary: Galaxy cluster formation is a self-similar and scale-free process of gravitational collapse. However, the thermodynamic properties of the intracluster medium often deviate from self-similar predictions. We investigate these deviations using a sample of 92 galaxy clusters selected through their Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect signal, spanning a mass range of $M_{500c}=[0.5-20] \times 10^{14}{M}_{\odot}$, and with redshifts $0.08 < z < 1.13$. Adopting a flexible framework that allows for radial variations in both redshift and mass scaling, we characterise the behaviour of scaled density, temperature, pressure, and entropy profiles, while simultaneously constraining their intrinsic scatter. We detect significant radial deviations from self-similar expectations in both redshift and mass scalings in all profiles. These deviations are strongest in the core regions, but remain measurable out to large radii ($\sim R_{500c}$), indicating that cluster outer regions are not fully described by purely gravitational evolution. We investigate the impact of an offset, a mass-dependence, and increased scatter between the mass proxy and the true mass on the radial mass scaling, finding that while its shape remains stable, its normalisation depends on the latter two effects. The pressure is the only thermodynamic quantity that exhibits approximately self-similar behaviour: outside the core it evolves self-similarly, with no dependence on mass. The entropy exhibits the strongest deviations from self-similarity as a function of radius. The intrinsic scatter peaks in the central regions and reaches a minimum at intermediate radii ($\lesssim 20 \%$ at $\sim 0.2$-$0.8 \ R_{500c}$), making this range optimal to reduce scatter in scaling relations. We conclude that the thermodynamic distributions exhibit non-self similar, mass-dependent scaling extending well beyond the core regime.

new.title: A Genetic Algorithm Approach to Reconstructing Scalar-Tensor Lagrangians
new.summary: Recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data, combined with cosmic microwave background (CMB) and Type Ia supernovae observations, have been interpreted as evidence for dynamical dark energy whose equation of state crosses the phantom divide $w=-1$. Such a crossing cannot be realized smoothly by a minimally coupled scalar field $\varphi$, but can arise naturally in scalar-tensor theories. We present a data-driven framework that reconstructs the scalar-tensor Lagrangian directly from observations, using a genetic algorithm to evolve the symbolic expressions for the nonminimal coupling $F(\varphi)$ and the scalar potential $U(\varphi)$. Each candidate is evaluated through a forward model that self-consistently determines the expansion history, the effective gravitational coupling, and the growth of structure. Candidates are ranked by a joint likelihood of DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+ supernovae calibrated with SH0ES Cepheids, compressed CMB distance priors, and redshift-space distortion measurements of $f\sigma_8$. We restrict to the unscreened branch of the theory and impose Solar System constraints on the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$ and on the time variation of the gravitational coupling, together with a Big Bang nucleosynthesis bound on its evolution. Across 64 independent runs, the best reconstruction improves the fit relative to $\Lambda$CDM by $\Delta\chi^2=-16.6$, compared with $\Delta\chi^2=-10.6$ for the CPL dark-energy parametrization. The preferred coupling is well described by $F(\varphi)=c_1\varphi^2+e^{\varphi}(1-c_2\varphi)$. The reconstructed theory shows phantom behavior at $z\gtrsim0.5$, but it remains close to $w=-1$ at low redshift.

new.title: Probing Dynamical Dark Energy with Hyper Suprime-Cam Year 3 Cosmic Shear
new.summary: Recent measurements of baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) and Type Ia Supernovae (SNe) have revealed a preference for a time-evolving dark energy equation of state. Because such dynamical behavior alters both the cosmic expansion history and the late-time growth of structure, weak gravitational lensing measurements can be used to test these extended models. We present an extended analysis of the real-space cosmic shear two-point correlation functions (2PCFs) from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Year 3 (HSC-Y3) survey. Using over 25 million galaxies across 416 deg$^2$, divided into four tomographic redshift bins ($0.3 < z \le 1.5$), we constrain both a constant ($w$CDM) and a time-varying ($w_0w_a$CDM) dark energy equation of state. To break the geometric degeneracies inherent in cosmic shear, we combine the HSC-Y3 data with a CMB-independent suite of background distance probes: DESI DR2 BAO, the recalibrated DES five-year SN sample (DOVEKIE), and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) priors. In the $w$CDM paradigm, our joint analysis yields $w =-0.936^{+0.074}_{-0.067}$, consistent with a cosmological constant. Within the $w_0w_a$CDM framework, we find $w_0 =-0.832^{+0.071}_{-0.059}$ and $w_a = -1.23^{+0.66}_{-0.44}$, representing a $2.4\sigma$ preference for dynamical dark energy. Although the unconstrained dark energy parameters reduce the cosmic shear-only $S_8$ constraints to smaller values, our joint multi-probe analysis agrees with the baseline HSC-Y3 $\Lambda$CDM structure growth amplitude. We obtain $S_8 = 0.774^{+0.027}_{-0.034}$ for $w$CDM and $S_8 = 0.772^{+0.031}_{-0.030}$ for $w_0w_a$CDM. Our results demonstrate that the weak lensing amplitude is robust to extended dark energy parameterizations, and that the dynamical dark energy signal is currently driven primarily by the geometric distance ladders, a critical consistency test for next-generation Stage-IV cosmological surveys.

new.title: Signals from the early Universe: primordial features from the full-shape analysis of BOSS galaxies and eBOSS quasars in combination with Planck
new.summary: We search for primordial oscillatory features using cosmic microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure (LSS) data, combining \textit{Planck} Public Release 4 (PR4) with galaxy clustering from the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) and quasars from the extended Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (eBOSS). For the LSS data we perform a full-shape analysis of the power spectrum multipoles with the one-loop effective field theory of large-scale structure, applying infrared resummation separately to each oscillatory component. We consider four templates: linearly and logarithmically oscillating features in Fourier space, with constant, localised, or power-law-decaying amplitudes, and fit them to the CMB and LSS data separately and jointly. We find no statistically significant evidence for primordial features in either dataset, individually or in combination. The best-fitting LSS features improve the fit by $\Delta\chi^2\simeq-6$ to $-10$, which corresponds to global significances of at most $1.6\,\sigma$ once the look-elsewhere effect is accounted for. In the CMB alone, the most significant feature is reduced to $\sim2.6\,\sigma$. Over the full frequency range, the LSS bounds on the feature amplitudes are weaker than those from \textit{Planck} by factors of $1.4$--$3$. Combining \textit{Planck} with \textit{BOSS+eBOSS} leaves the CMB constraints essentially unchanged, because the LSS data do not favour the frequencies preferred by the CMB.

cross.title: Anisotropic Fluid Inhomogeneous Cosmology
cross.summary: We propose a new framework for inhomogeneous cosmology based on General Relativity sourced by an anisotropic fluid. The model is parametrized by a single input function, the radial Misner--Sharp mass distribution at different redshifts, and admits exact solutions to Einstein's equations. Going beyond the standard assumption of small metric perturbations, it provides a fully relativistic framework to describe the non-linear regime of cosmic structure formation. The Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) cosmology is recovered both at early times and -- on large scales only -- at late times. Our Anisotropic Fluid Inhomogeneous Cosmology (AFIC) model provides a natural mechanism through which matter inhomogeneities give rise to late-time acceleration. The extensive term driving this effect does not enter the exact metric solution and therefore does not contribute to the local gravitational potential. Rather, it emerges as a genuinely large-scale effect induced by the inhomogeneous distribution of matter at late times. This mechanism may provide a physical interpretation of the results from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). Finally, we present a simple analytical realization of the model and use it to provide an estimate of the present-day effective dark energy density.

cross.title: Toward Automated Strong-Lens Modeling with Agentic Workflows: An Application to Euclid Q1 Lenses
cross.summary: Ongoing and forthcoming wide-field surveys will discover $O(10^5)$ galaxy-galaxy strong lenses, shifting the main bottleneck from detection to reliable physical modeling. Conventional forward-modeling pipelines still rely on case-by-case expert judgment and manual tuning to mask contaminants, initialize priors, diagnose unphysical fits, and reconfigure failed runs. We present Lens-Orchestra, an automated workflow coupling a team of multimodal large language model agents to multi-stage physical modeling with elliptical power-law mass profiles, external shear, and pixelized source reconstructions. Launched via natural-language instructions, it modeled 185 Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1) grade-A lens candidates with published mass models without human intervention, completing 149 fits. Independent human evaluation confirmed 140 usable models, including 126 grade-I fits with noise-level residuals (with only 6.0% of completed fits unacceptable), and endorsed all 36 halted runs. Across the 140 usable systems, effective Einstein radii match released Q1 models (+0.12% median offset; 2.73% typical scatter), while hierarchical inference on the 126 grade-I imaging-only fits yields a mean mass-density slope of $2.002 \pm 0.009$ (intrinsic scatter $0.074^{+0.007}_{-0.006}$). A dedicated residual-screening agent also guided the selection of two candidate low-mass perturbers for parametric and free-form substructure modeling; although neither was confirmed, this end-to-end search illustrates how automated screening focuses computationally intensive substructure analyses on a few promising systems. Coupling multimodal agents to explicit forward modeling thus enables accurate, survey-scale lens analysis from macro mass profiles to small-scale dark matter structure.

cross.title: Moon Radio Interferometer for Science and Exploration (MoonRISE): A Mission Concept for a Low-Frequency Radio Interferometer on the Lunar Farside
cross.summary: The universe below 20 MHz remains one of space science's last unexplored frontiers, inaccessible from Earth due to its ionosphere and terrestrial radio frequency interference (RFI). We present the mission concept for the Moon Radio Interferometer for Science and Exploration (MoonRISE), an all-sky imaging, low-frequency radio telescope operating from 100 kHz-30 MHz from the lunar farside, the quietest radio environment in the inner Solar System. If realized, MoonRISE would be the first radio interferometer on the Moon and the first connected-element radio interferometer in space. Its science objectives are to (1) determine how solar wind turbulence drives plasma heating, acceleration, and space weather evolution in the inner heliosphere, by measuring the scattering of type III solar radio bursts between 2-20 solar radii; (2) constrain the density, structure, and variability of the lunar ionosphere and its effects on surface communication; and (3) resolve the plasma sources and magnetospheric dynamics that power Uranian Kilometric Radiation, observable for the first time since Voyager 2 in 1986. The same observations would yield all-sky maps of the low-frequency sky, subsurface structure at the landing site, and a characterization of the farside RF environment. The Radio Interferometer concept consists of nine 3.5 m dipoles embedded in a 1.5 km optical-fiber tether deployed by a rover, with power- and RF-over-fiber enabling RFI-free mapping. A rover-mounted Ground Penetrating Radar (300-2000 MHz) would measure regolith dielectric properties and bedrock depth to characterize the dipoles' RF performance. We describe the science objectives, a reference landing site in Lacus Luxuriae, a notional concept of operations, and the payload design and technology maturity. The concept builds on SunRISE and OVRO-LWA heritage and could serve as a basis for a future selected mission.

cross.title: Environmental resonances in extreme-mass-ratio inspirals within boson clouds
cross.summary: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) offer a promising probe of matter environments around massive black holes through gravitational-wave (GW) observations. We investigate orbital resonances induced by conservative gravitational perturbations from such environments. Combining a multiparameter expansion with the action-angle formalism, we derive a general resonance condition for generic bound Kerr orbits. Applying this framework to ultralight scalar clouds formed through black hole superradiance, we show that orbital resonances can arise from a single-mode cloud without requiring transitions between cloud modes. Our analysis demonstrates that these resonances can lead to significant GW dephasing, providing a new avenue for probing boson clouds through GWs and highlighting the importance of including environmental resonances in accurate EMRI waveform modeling.

cross.title: Black hole accretion flows as dark matter bolometers
cross.summary: Astrophysical systems provide powerful probes of dark matter interactions, complementing direct-detection searches. We propose using accretion flows of the supermassive black hole as a bolometer for light DM. The kinetic energy of sub-MeV dark matter in the black hole gravitational potential can remain below the thermal energy of the plasma electrons. The colder dark matter population can therefore absorb energy through elastic scattering, cooling the electrons and modifying their emission spectrum. We integrate dark matter cooling into the advection-dominated accretion flow around M87$^{*}$ and solve the full set of thermodynamic equations to obtain the resulting temperature profile and radio-to-millimeter emission. By comparing the predicted spectrum with observations accompanying the Event Horizon Telescope campaign, we use, for the first time, the thermal energy balance of the hot accretion flow to constrain DM-electron scattering, obtaining stringent limits on keV-to-MeV DM for both heavy and light mediators.

cross.title: Inverted Pendulum in the Sky: Floquet Stabilization of Cosmological Axions
cross.summary: Many cosmological scenarios require a scalar field to sit near the top of its potential, which usually requires a fine-tuned initial condition. We ask whether the hilltop of an axion potential can be dynamically stabilized by a rapidly oscillating coupling, as for the inverted pendulum of Kapitza, and to what extent this can reduce the fine-tuning. Using Floquet theory, we determine the stability window of the hilltop and analyze several realizations: an oscillating coupling, a spinning or oscillating second field, and a gyroscopic analogue, an inverted spinning top realized by a sigma model on a squashed three-sphere. In an expanding Universe the stabilized phase lasts for a number of $e$-folds logarithmic in the hierarchy of scales, independently of the cosmological background. Classifying the stabilizers by how their effective frequency redshifts, we show that in these realizations the hilltop cannot both attract the field and leave it frozen by the Hubble friction during radiation or matter domination, and that during inflation the attraction is limited by the Hubble friction and the energy budget. Thus the simple realizations studied here do not generically remove the hilltop fine-tuning. They can instead delay the onset of the oscillation and enhance the relic abundance as $n_\phi/n_{\phi,{\rm std}}\propto(\tilde m/H_c)^{3/2}$ in radiation domination. We discuss the implications for axion dark matter, inflation, quintessence and curvatons.

repl.title: Accurate parameter inference for the Light-cone Epoch of Reionization 21-cm signal
repl.summary: The light-cone (LC) effect breaks the statistical homogeneity along the line-of-sight (LoS) direction of the 21-cm signal. Consequently, the traditional power spectrum (PS) fundamentally fails to capture the full two-point statistical information. The evolving power spectrum (ePS) offers an alternative, explicitly accounting for the LoS evolution due to the LC effect while maintaining physical interpretability. We compare the statistical constraining power of three different summary statistics: the standard cylindrical PS $P(k_\perp,k_\parallel)$, slice-wise PS $P_s(k, z)$ (1D-PS computed over small bandwidth LC slices), and ePS $P_e(k, z)$. We first demonstrate that $P_e(k,z)$ successfully recovers the benchmark 1D-PS of coeval simulations across all scales and redshifts, whereas the slice-wise PS only recovers the 1D-PS at small scales. To efficiently perform parameter inference, we train artificial neural network (ANN) emulators on $500$ simulated LC 21-cm signals. Our forecasts incorporate cosmic variance, estimated using $50$ statistically independent realizations of the signal, alongside SKA-Low system noise for integration times of $1000$ and $104$ hours. We demonstrate that the ePS outperforms its peers, yielding credible intervals that are $\sim 3$ and $\sim 1.4$ times tighter than those obtained using $P(k_\perp,k_\parallel)$ and $P_s(k,z)$, respectively. These results establish the ePS as an optimal summary statistic for interpreting forthcoming large-bandwidth LC 21-cm observations.

repl.title: Sensitive 3mm Imaging of Discrete Sources in the Fields of X-ray-Selected Galaxy Clusters
repl.summary: In this paper, we present the results of a blind survey for compact sources in 138 galaxy clusters from the eFEDS X-ray survey. Of these clusters, 96 are new observations. These targets have X-ray mass estimates and redshifts that formally place them above the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect (tSZ) survey limits from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT, DR5), yet were not detected. Compact sources with apparent locations close to (<104") the center of a galaxy cluster can in-fill the tSZ flux decrement, resulting in tSZ surveys missing clusters. To quantify the number of missing clusters from ACT, we carried out a survey at 90GHz using MUSTANG2 on the Green Bank Telescope and achieved a 5-sigma detection limit of 1mJy in the center of each cluster. We detected 11 discrete sources, which when scaled, is slightly lower than our previous tSZ selected sample, M2-ACT (8.0% vs 9.9%). All had radio counterparts. However, unlike the M2-ACT sample, the sources in X-ray selected clusters were concentrated closer to the cluster centers. When their effect on the measured tSZ signal is taken into account the sources we found would result in 4.5% of clusters being missed by tSZ surveys - a result similar to the estimate in recent ACT results. Most of the 96 clusters in eFEDS but not in ACT are a result of noise and overestimation of mass from X-ray measurements.

repl.title: Two-dimensional weak lensing shear for cluster mass, concentration, ellipticity and miscentering estimation
repl.summary: The effects of weak gravitational lensing induced by clusters of galaxies makes it possible to constrain their dark matter distribution. In general mass estimates from weak lensing are made by compressing the two-dimensional shear-field into one-dimension. In this work we build a forward model of the two-dimensional reduced-shear field around a galaxy cluster, including the non-Gaussian correlated large-scale structure from N-body simulations, the uncorrelated line-of-sight structure, cluster miscentering and ellipticity. We then use simulation-based inference to obtain posteriors on the cluster mass, concentration, miscentering and ellipticity from the full field. The two-dimensional approach leads to improvements on cluster mass constraints by up to 20\%. We show that this is due to a better treatment of the spatially correlated noise across the shear field. There is also significant improvements on the cluster concentration and miscentering. Whilst improvements are also made to the estimation of cluster ellipticity, the constraints are still prior dependent for these individual cluster constraints. We also quantify the impact of the line-of-sight structure on the constraints. Neglecting it underestimates the mass uncertainty by up to a factor of $2$ for the most massive clusters.

repl.title: Targeting the future of spectroscopic galaxy surveys -- A cosmological study case with the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope
repl.summary: The next generation of Stage-V spectroscopic surveys are designed to measure hundreds of millions of galaxy and quasar spectra, extending precision large-scale-structure cosmology to redshifts and volumes well beyond the reach of current Stage-IV facilities. Realising this potential requires revisiting the target selection strategies and designing them explicitly around the depth, multiplexing, and survey time of the new instruments, rather than a direct extrapolation of existing recipes. This work develops and characterises new strategies for the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST), a proposed 12-metre, highly multiplexed facility expected to operate in the 2040s. Using deep multi-band photometry, including COSMOS-field data from CLAUDS and HSC, we revisit low-redshift $z \lesssim 1.6$ tracer selection of SDSS, BOSS/eBOSS, DESI and 4MOST-CRS -- Bright Galaxies, Luminous Red Galaxies, Emission Line Galaxies and quasars -- to photometric depth achievable in the WST era, and introduce a purely magnitude-limited sample (MagMax) exploiting three-dimensional color-color star-galaxy separation, and a set of Lyman-Break Galaxy dropout samples extending target selection to $z \gtrsim 2$. Using Fisher-matrix forecasts, we showcase the constraining power of a WST-like cosmological survey on BAO distance parameters $\alpha_\parallel$ and $\alpha_\perp$, the growth rate $f$, the evolving dark energy equation $w_0w_a$, the local-type primordial non-Gaussianity $f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc}$, and the sum of the neutrino mass $\Sigma m_\nu$. The main outcome of this work is an optimisation framework that directly links instrumental capabilities and observing time to cosmological constraining power, providing a science-driven template applicable to the design of future generations of Stage-V spectroscopic surveys.

repl.title: Towards modelling redshift uncertainties in the photometric void size function
repl.summary: We present an extension of the theoretical formalism for the Void Size Function (VSF) to incorporate photometric redshift uncertainties, combining the excursion set with the theory of Lagrangian density peaks. Photometric redshift scatter induces anisotropic line-of-sight smoothing of the density field, which modifies the variance of the field and suppresses the abundance of large voids. We model this effect by damping the variance of the smoothed density field in the theoretical model, and we test it on AbacusSummit halo lightcones with true redshifts and with mock photometric redshifts generated with a Gaussian scatter. The predicted damping of the variance agrees with the one measured in the halo distribution to 1% and the suppression of the VSF due to photometric redshift scatter is well reproduced by the modified model, with recalibrated barrier parameters, for sigma_z <= 0.015 and for voids larger than 40 Mpc/h (about 2.5 mean tracer separations). This work is a first step towards modelling the VSF in modern photometric surveys such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time and the Euclid mission.

repl.title: The Simons Observatory: Analysis of methods for polarization calibration of multiple instruments
repl.summary: Cosmic birefringence, the rotation of the CMB linear polarization plane across the Universe, is a powerful test of parity-violating physics beyond the Standard Model. Static isotropic rotation, however, is limited by an instrument's absolute polarization-angle calibration. We present a method for transferring absolute calibration between Simons Observatory (SO) instruments, validated on map-level simulations of the Large Aperture Telescope (LAT) and Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs) with lensed CMB polarization, polarized Galactic foregrounds, correlated instrumental noise, and polarization-angle miscalibration. We develop two pipelines: a joint LAT+SAT likelihood transferring calibration through their overlap, and the Minami-Komatsu foreground-based method, which separates cosmic birefringence from instrumental miscalibration using Galactic dust polarization without an external angle prior. We derive a general variance budget showing that calibration transfer improves sensitivity only when the combined reference and overlap transfer uncertainties remain below the receiving instrument's calibration uncertainty. While transfer does not lower the absolute-angle floor for isotropic $\beta$, it anchors the receiving instrument's multipole range. The relative-angle uncertainty is $\sim 0.1^\circ$ for $\ell_{\max}^{\mathrm{SAT}}=300$, improving to $\sim 0.04^\circ$ at $\ell_{\max}^{\mathrm{SAT}}=600$, subject to SAT beam and transfer-function control. Finally, for $\beta=0.3^\circ$, we show how the LAT's $\ell$-range distinguishes scale-independent dark-energy rotation from scale-dependent axion dark-matter models via $C_\ell^{EB}$.

repl.title: Smooth binary evolution from wide resonances in boson clouds
repl.summary: Ultralight scalars can form superradiant clouds around rotating black holes. These may alter the dynamics of compact binaries and the ensuing waveform through orbital resonances and cloud ionization. We re-examine resonances involving states with nonzero decay width, deriving an effective treatment for resonances that are wider than the binary's frequency chirp. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by calculating an upper bound for the cloud's mass surviving up to the latest stages of the inspiral. Next, we study the accumulation of resonances with high-energy bound states. When these infinitely many, increasingly weak resonances are properly taken into account, they smooth out the "sharp features" in the binary's evolution that had been attributed to the ionization of the cloud. We compare our Newtonian results with recent relativistic calculations, highlighting common features as well as discrepancies. Our conclusions emphasize the need to carefully incorporate resonances in boson cloud waveform modeling.

repl.title: Acoustic gravitational waves from primordial curvature perturbations
repl.summary: Standard perturbative calculations of scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) have neglected nonperturbative effects in the large-amplitude regime. We develop a hybrid numerical framework to signify nonperturbative effects on the stochastic gravitational wave (GW) background sourced by primordial curvature perturbations, focusing on the acoustic channel (fluid motions). Fully general-relativistic, spherically symmetric simulations are used to extract nonperturbative sound-shell profiles from isolated curvature peaks; these profiles are then embedded into three-dimensional lattice evolutions of relativistic hydrodynamics coupled to transverse-traceless metric perturbations to compute the acoustic GW spectra. The acoustic signal has a peak frequency determined by the comoving shell thickness, and its amplitude is extremely sensitive to the mean comoving separation of peaks, scaling approximately as $R_{*c}^{-7}$. We find a robust causal low-frequency tail $\propto k^{3}$, and the nonlinear hydrodynamic interactions can enhance the ultraviolet power. Comparing with SIGWs computed perturbatively from the same real-space configuration, we show that acoustic GWs can be amplified by an order of magnitude and display a peak shifted to a lower frequency in the large-amplitude regime. These results highlight the importance of nonperturbative effects for accurate predictions of stochastic GW signals induced from primordial curvature perturbations.

repl.title: Dark matter in classically conformal theories: WIMP and supercooling
repl.summary: Beyond solving the hierarchy problem, classically conformal (CC) theories naturally accommodate dark matter (DM). In this work, we explore the CC $SU(2)_X$ gauge theory with a triplet dark scalar, uncovering two distinct DM scenarios: weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) and supercooled DM. The production mechanisms are strongly influenced by the CC model's unique first-order phase transition evolution history, which differs significantly from those in non-conformal models. We obtain the viable parameter space for each scenario and investigate the current constraints and future sensitivities at experiments, demonstrating that gravitational wave signals from the phase transition provide a common detection channel for both the WIMP and supercooled DM regimes.

repl.title: Hyrax: An Extensible Framework for Rapid ML Experimentation and Unsupervised Discovery in the Era of Rubin, Roman, and Euclid
repl.summary: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Roman Space Telescope, Euclid, and other next-generation surveys will deliver imaging, spectroscopic, and time-domain data at scales that increasingly shift the bottleneck in astronomical machine learning (ML) projects from model design to infrastructure. We present Hyrax, an open-source, modular, GPU-enabled Python framework that supports the full ML lifecycle in astronomy: from data acquisition and training to inference and experiment comparison, with capabilities including multimodal dataset support, integrated vector databases for similarity search, and interactive two- and three-dimensional latent-space exploration for unsupervised discovery. We demonstrate Hyrax's versatility through five representative applications on real survey data: (i) unsupervised representation learning on $\sim 4\times10^5$ Rubin Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) Data Preview 1 (DP1) galaxies, surfacing new merger and low-surface-brightness candidates missing from reference Euclid and Dark Energy Survey catalogs, while also isolating imaging artifacts -- all without labeled training data; (ii) hybrid density-based clustering for identifying cluster-scale gravitational lens candidates in DP1 data; (iii) multimodal early-time transient classification in the Zwicky Transient Facility leveraging light curves, spectra, images, and metadata; (iv) supervised false-positive filtering in shift-and-stack searches for distant solar system objects in the Dark Energy Camera Ecliptic Exploration Project survey; and (v) supervised detection of semi-resolved dwarf galaxies in Hyper Suprime-Cam and LSST-like imaging using synthetic source injection. Together, these results demonstrate that Hyrax provides astronomy-specific ML infrastructure that enables systematic discovery and rapid methodological iteration across next-generation astronomical surveys.

repl.title: On Cross-Correlating Line Intensity Maps from SPHEREx during Reionization
repl.summary: We have simulated Ly{\alpha}, H{\alpha}, H{\beta}, [OII], and [OIII] intensity maps which are observable by SPHEREx during cosmic reionization. We simulate these intensity maps including all significant sources of emission for each line, and include radiative transfer for the Ly{\alpha} intensity maps. We also include a simple model of dust extinction based on observations of galaxies at z<5. One of the main challenges of intensity mapping is interloping lines from galaxies at lower redshifts, which makes producing an auto-power spectrum challenging. We focus on cross-correlations between different lines, as this eliminates such foreground contamination of the signal. We have cross-correlated the simulated SPHEREx intensity maps to find the most observable cases. This includes modeling of interloping lines and masking bright interloping galaxies. repl.title: XRISM Reveals a Kinematically Coherent Core System of the Nearby Cool-Core Cluster Abell 2199
repl.summary: We present the results of a deep 251 ks XRISM/Resolve observation of the cool core of the galaxy cluster Abell 2199. From the integrated spectrum of the central $3' \times 3'$ Resolve field of view ($104 \times 104 \mathrm{~kpc}^2$), we find that the intracluster medium (ICM) redshift is consistent with that of the brightest cluster galaxy, within the optical-redshift uncertainty. This indicates that they form a kinematically coherent core system, which is offset from the mean cluster redshift by $\sim200~\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$. The observed velocity dispersion of $\sim100~\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$ corresponds to a three-dimensional Mach number of $M_{\mathrm{3D}}=0.16$ and a non-thermal pressure fraction of $P_{\mathrm{NT}}/P_{\mathrm{tot}}=1.4\pm0.2$%. Abell 2199 is one of the most dynamically quiescent relaxed clusters observed with XRISM, despite the presence of radio jets and a plume-like structure possibly associated with sloshing motions. Order-of-magnitude estimates suggest that turbulent dissipation could offset a non-negligible fraction of the radiative cooling losses, with $Q_{\mathrm{turb}}/Q_{\mathrm{cool}}\approx0.1$ for a large-scale driver such as sloshing and larger values for smaller AGN-feedback scales. Finally, we detect a localized enhancement of the Fe XXV He$\alpha$ $y$ line in the southeast region, which spatially coincides with a Chandra surface brightness discontinuity.

repl.title: Galaxy mergers drive enhancements in ionization states
repl.summary: Recent studies have suggested that galaxy mergers may help drive the escape of ionizing photons from galaxies. However, the ionization properties of merging galaxies have not yet been systematically studied across the full merger sequence in a large, well-defined sample. Here, we investigate the impact of mergers on the line ratio $\rm{O}_{32}$ tracing the ionization state and study its evolution as a function of merger progression. We identify 7641 galaxy mergers with robust (SNR > 3) emission line fluxes from the SDSS DR 17, using spectroscopic pair analysis and visual classifications from the participatory science experiment "Cosmic Disco: Characterizing Galaxy Collision". We find a continuous increase in $\rm{O}_{32}$ as a function of merger progression traced by pair separation and visual merger stages, with median and 90th percentile peaking post-coalescence. $\rm{O}_{32}$ is significantly enhanced in mergers past the first pericenter passage as compared to a control sample of isolated galaxies. We investigate the properties of galaxy mergers with $\rm{O}_{32}$ > 3 and find that these are mainly low-mass ($\widetilde{\rm{M}_{*}}=6\times 10^{8}\,\rm{M}{_\odot}$) mergers near coalescence. In this population, large $\rm{O}_{32}$ values are due to mergers driving a simultaneous increase in specific star formation rate and decrease in metallicity. Thus, galaxy mergers enhance the ionization state of galaxies and likely facilitate the escape of ionizing radiation from galaxies, even at low stellar masses. Finally, we infer that Green Pea galaxies, a population characterized by high O32, could possibly be low-mass galaxy mergers at or close-to coalescence, a scenario that would reconcile findings from environmental and interferometric 21cm studies.

repl.title: StAGE: Stellar Archaeology-driven Galaxy Evolution II. Binary Black Hole Mergers in Quiescent Galaxies and their Star-forming Progenitors
repl.summary: We apply StAGE, a data-driven galaxy-evolution framework based on stellar archaeology, to study binary black hole (BBH) mergers associated with present-day quiescent galaxies (QGs) and their star-forming progenitors. By combining StAGE star-formation and chemical-enrichment histories with pre-computed SEVN population-synthesis catalogs, we predict the BBH merger-rate density, intrinsic binary properties, merger-time host-galaxy distributions, and the associated stochastic gravitational-wave (GW) background. A distinctive feature of StAGE is that it jointly tracks the stellar-binary environment at birth and the properties of the host galaxy at merger time. Moreover, stellar-archaeology constraints on $\alpha$-enhancement allow us to explore how adopting the iron abundance relevant for massive-star winds, rather than oxygen-based total metallicity, affects the predicted BBH merger rates. We find that most BBHs form at moderately subsolar metallicities $Z\lesssim Z_\odot/3$, while their merger-time hosts typically have stellar masses $M_\star\sim10^{10}-10^{11.5}\,M_\odot$ at $z\lesssim2$. At and beyond cosmic noon, hosts lie mainly on the star-forming main sequence, whereas starbursting and quenching descendants contribute increasingly toward lower redshift. Using the independent approach offered by StAGE, we also confirm recent literature findings that, for most binary-evolution prescriptions, predicted local BBH merger rates exceed the LVK-inferred range, while dynamical formation in stellar clusters extends the BBH primary mass distribution into the high-mass regime poorly populated by isolated binaries. Finally, the predicted stochastic background approaches the projected sensitivity of planned LVK upgrades and lies within reach of the Einstein Telescope. All in all, StAGE can provide physically motivated host priors for GW-source localization and dark-siren cosmology.

repl.title: HydróDex: gotta match 'em all!
repl.summary: First-order phase transitions can source a stochastic gravitational-wave background within reach of LISA and other future detectors, with sound waves in the plasma typically providing the dominant contribution. Predicting the resulting gravitational-wave signal requires determining the stationary fluid profiles around expanding bubbles. We present a complete hydrodynamic classification of these profiles in the constant-sound-speed model, which generalizes the bag model by allowing the sound speeds in front of and behind the wall, $c_+$ and $c_-$, to differ. Solving the matching conditions at the wall and evolving the surrounding plasma, we recover the known direct and inverse detonations, deflagrations, and hybrids, and uncover mixed hybrids, a new class with rarefaction waves on both sides of the wall and oppositely directed fluid flows. For a sufficiently pronounced hierarchy $c_+>c_-$, multiple stationary profiles can correspond to the same wall velocity $\xi_w$ and asymptotic transition strength $\alpha_N$. This non-uniqueness arises because this parametrization discards thermodynamic information and is resolved once the underlying microphysics is specified. We compute the kinetic-energy budget and acoustic gravitational-wave spectra within the sound-shell model, finding that mixed hybrids introduce no additional spectral feature and can be mimicked by ordinary direct or inverse hybrids with substantially different fluid profiles. Finally, we release HydróDex, a public code implementing the complete classification, profile construction, energy-budget calculation, and gravitational-wave prediction.
